3.  Findings to Continue to Hold Remote TeleconferenceNirtual City Council Meetings
  Pursuant to Assembly Bill 361
  At the November 16, 2021 City Council meeting, the City Council made findings pursuant
  to Assembly Bill 361 to continue to meet remotely. To continue this practice, it is required,
  that the City Council determine that the COVID-19 state of emergency proclaimed by the
  Governor still exists and has been considered by the City Council in deciding to continue
  to have teleconference meetings and that state or local offidals have imposed or
  recommended measures to promote social distancing in connection with COVID-19, and
  that as a result of the COVID-19 emergency, meeting in person would present imminent
  risks to the health or safety of attendees. Because these findings must be made every
  thirty (30) days, the City Council will have to make these findings at its upcoming June 8,
  2022 meeting and thirty (30) days thereafter.
  Recommended Action
  Determine that the COVID-1 9 state of emergency proclaimed by the Governor still exists
  and has been considered by the City Council in deciding to continue to have
  teleconference meetings and that state or local officials have imposed or recommended
  measures to promote social distancing in connection with COVID-19, and that as a result
  of the COVID-19 emergency, meeting in person would present imminent risks to the
  health or safety of attendees.

4.  Declare Excess/Old Equipment as Surplus
  Historically, the City Council is presented with a list of items that are surplus, the Council
  declares it surplus, and then the declared items are either sold via Public Surplus, given
  to charity, or disposed of properly.
  Recommended Action
  Adopt a resolution declaring equipment listed in resolution as surplus property and
  authorize the City Manager to dispose of it in accordance with City policy.

5.  Catalina Island Yacht Club Lease
  On May 3, 2022, City Staff were provided with a proposal from the Catalina Island Yacht
  Club (CIYC). The proposal requests the City and CIYC enter into a new long-term lease
  agreement that would allow CIYC to justify necessary improvements to its facility at 30
  Casino Way, and align with the Tuna Club.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize the City Manager to negotiate with the Catalina Island Yacht Club to terminate
  the existing lease and subscription agreement and execute a new lease with revised
  terms.

6.  Approve Professional Services Agreement for Avalon Mode Shift Feasibility Study
  Avalon City Council accepted a grant on August 4, 2020 from the California Department
  of Transportation to study strategies that will enable the city to develop a multimodal
  transportation strategy to reduce reliance on personal motor vehicles, enhance the City’s
  public transportation services, and guide implementation of recommendations from the
  City’s previously completed Active Transportation Plan. The grant requirements require a
  competitive solicitation focused on the grant. A request for proposals was solicited and
  closed on May 20, 2022. W-Trans was the only firm to submit a proposal.
  Recommended Action
  Approve a Professional Services Agreement for the Avalon Mode Shift Feasibility Study
  for a not to exceed cost of $160000 with W-Trans, Inc.

PUBLIC HEARING

7.  Fiscal Year 2022-2023 Miscellaneous Fee Schedule Workshop
  The City charges fees for miscellaneous public services, facility use/rental and activities.
  User fees are assessed and collected for City services and programs provided by various
  departments. These are services that convey a benefit, grant a privilege, provide for
  review and enforcement of regulatory activities, enforce laws or are a condition of
  development. Under State law, cities may charge fees to recoup the direct and indirect
  costs related to the provision of user services.
  Recommended Action
  1. Open the Public Hearing to hear public comments. 2. Close the Public Hearing. 3.
  Discuss and determine an appropriate fee increase. 4. If consensus, adopt the fee
  schedule.
 CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
JUNE 8, 2022
PAGE 5

8.  Appeal Planning Commission Action 22-01 of PC #2783 Approving a Setback Variance
  at 261 E. Whittley
  On April 20,2022, the Planning Commission of the City of Avalon took action on a request
  for approval of a Site Plan and a Setback Variance at 261 E. Whittley for the ongoing
  remodel of a duplex in the Medium Density Residential zone. On May 3, 2022 Charles
  Canby. and other surrounding property owners, filed a timely appeal of the Planning
  Commission’s decision, requesting that the City Council hear the Project at a public
  hearing.
  Recommended Action
  1. Open the Public Hearing to hear public comment. 2. Close the Public Hearing. 3.
  Discuss and determine appropriate action by either a.) Affirm the action of the Planning
  Commission; b.) Require a transcript or recording of the testimony, and all other evidence
  upon which the Commission made its decision, and after receiving such evidence take
  such action as, in its opinion, is indicated by such evidence alone; c.) Refer the matter
  back to the Commission, with or without instructions for further proceedings; or d.)
  Continue the matter for hearing on another date before itself. (Avalon Municipal Code
  Section 9-8.601)

SUBJECT:  Findings to Continue to Hold Remote TeleconferenceNirtual City
  Council Meetings Pursuant to Assembly Bill 361

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Determine that the COVID-19 state of emergency proclaimed
by the Governor still exists and has been considered by the City Council in deciding to continue
to have teleconference meetings and that state or local officials have imposed or recommended
measures to promote social distancing in connection with COVID-19, and that as a result of the
COVID-19 emergency, meeting in person would present imminent risks to the health or safety
of attendees.

REPORT SUMMARY: Traditionallythe Brown Act allows for teleconference or virtual meetings,
provided that the physical locations of the legislative body’s members joining by teleconference
are posted on the agenda, that those locations are open to the public and that a quorum of the
members is located within its jurisdiction. Newly enacted AB 361 provides an exception to these
procedures in order to allow for fully virtual meetings during proclaimed emergencies, including
the COVID-19 pandemic.

Since March of 2020 and the issuance of Governor Newsoms Executive Order N-29-20, which
suspended portions of the Brown Act relating to teleconferencing, the City Council has had virtual
meetings without having to post the location of the legislative body members attending virtually.
Most public agencies have been holding public meetings using virtual platforms since this time.
In June of 2021 Governor Newsom issued Executive Order N-08-21, which provided that the
exceptions contained in EO N-29-20 would sunset on September 30, 2021.

On September 10, 2021, the Legislature adopted AB 361, which allows public agencies to hold
fully virtual meetings under certain circumstances without the posting of the agenda from each
location a legislative body member is attending. Governor Newsom signed the bill into law on
September 16, 2021. Because it contained an urgency provision, it took immediate effect.

Specific Findings Required underAB 361

Under AB 361, the City Council can hold virtual meetings without providing notice of the City
Council’s teleconference location if the City Council makes the determination that there is a
Governor-proclaimed state of emergency, which the City Council will consider in their
determination, and one of two secondary criteria listed below exists:

  1. State or local officials have imposed or recommended measures to promote social
  distancing in connection with COVID-19; or

65059.00000\3452048 1.1
   2, The City Council determines that requiring a meeting in person would present an
  imminent risk to the health or safety of attendees.

COVID-19 continues to present an imminent threat to the health or safety of members of the
public, and the Governor’s declaration of a CDVI D-19 emergency still exists. Although vaccines
are now widely available, many people in the State and County are still not fully vaccinated and
remain susceptible to infection. The disease can still spread rapidly through person-to-person
contact and those in close proximity. Further, more contagious variants of the disease are now
present in the State and County, the most predominant of which is a new variant of the Omnicron
variant, The County of Los Angeles recently re-instituted some mandates given the rise in cases
and deaths nationally. The City’s economy is dependent upon visitors to the island, the presence
of which, increases the likelihood of transmission of the disease. Also, having members of the
public attend council meetings at locations where council members are in attendance due to their
desire to avoid exposure to COVID-1 9 poses an imminent risk to the health or safety of attendees.

Re-Authorization is Required Within 30 Days

The City Council made the findings listed above at its May 17, 2022 City Council meeting.
Consistent with the provisions of Government Code Section 54953(e), the findings must be made
every 30 days “after teleconferencing for the first time” under AB 361. Thus, if the City Council
desires to continue to meet remotely without having to post the location of each teleconference
location, the City Council must again find that the CDVI D-19 emergency still exists and that one
of the two following findings can be made: that state or local officials have imposed or
recommended measures to promote social distancing in connection with COVID-19. or, that a
result of the CDVI D-19 emergency, meeting in person would present imminent risks to the health
or safety of attendees. Because these findings must be made every thirty (30) days, the City
Council will have to make these findings at its upcoming July 5, 2022 meeting and thirty (30)
days thereafter.

It is recommended that the City Council make these findings.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The City Council will
have to follow the Brown Act provisions that existed prior to the CDVID-1 9 pandemic.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: That the City Council make the findings under AB 361 at its July 5, 2022
City Council meeting.

SUBJECT:  Catalina Island Yacht Club Lease

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Authorize the City Manager negotiate with the Catalina Island
Yacht Club to terminate the existing lease and subscription agreement and execute a new
lease with revised terms.

REPORT SUMMARY: On May 3, 2022, City Staff were provided with a proposal from the
Catalina Island Yacht Club (CIYC). The proposal requests the City and CIYC enter into a new
tong-term tease agreement that would aflow CIYC to continue the substantial yearly
investments necessary to preserve” its facility at 30 Casino Way.

The CIYC has occupied the property at 30 Casino Way since August 24, 1924. More recently,
CIYC and the City of Avalon entered into its current lease and subscription agreement in 1995.
The initial term of the lease was 15 years with an additional 10 year extension. In 2006 the City
and CIYC entered into a first amendment to this lease and subscription agreement establishing
increasing the minimum donation from CIYC to benefit the City of Avalon and/or its residents
as well as establishing a new base rent rate.

In 2017. CIYC and the City enter into a second amendment to the lease and subscription
agreement. The second amendment:
  -  Extended the initial term of the lease to 2023 and extended the renewal term by 10
  years potentially extending the lease to 2033.
  -  Required the lease rate to be subject to annual CPI.
  -  Required CIYC to make improvements to maintain the structure at a minimum $30,000
  each year subject to annual CPI.
  -  Required the annual minimum pledge amount to increase by CPI each year.

In the May 3, 2022 proposal, CIYC requests a new 20 year lease term, with two 10-year
extension periods. If approved, this lease will align with the term granted to the Tuna Club in
2021 and would potential extend the CIYC lease to 2062.

Additionally, the proposal outlines a large number of capital improvement projects CIYC plans
to complete to improve its clubhouse. Included in the list of projects is installation of retaining
walls to mitigate potential rock slides caused by erosion to the hillside area facing the
clubhouse. CIYC wishes to partner with the City on this project and has allocated
approximately $160,000 to support this effort.
 It is anticipated that the retaining wall will create parking spaces opposite CIYC. The lease will
include a provision to designate the newly created parking spaces to run with the lease for
exclusive use by the CIYC.

City Staff recommend the City Council authorizes the City Manager to negotiate terms for a
new lease agreement with CIYC that establishes a new lease term, updates the overall lease
agreement to the City’s standard lease terms, and establishes terms for a partnership to
mitigate hillside issues and establish a parking area for the CIYC.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Undetermined.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: None.

  April 2022

Purpose

The Catalina Island Yacht Club, faced with the ongoing substantial financial obligations for
maintenance of the historic building at 30 Casino Way, is seeking a new long-term lease
agreement with the City of Avalon. This would allow The Club to continue the substantial yearly
investments necessary to preserve this historic building.

History

The Catalina Island Yacht Club (“CIYC”) was founded on March 7, 1924, by CIYC members Art
Sanger and James Jump in response to need for a social club on Santa Catalina Island open to
men and women alike that would complement the Tuna Club’s focus on angling sport. The CIYC
clubhouse also replaced the Sophia Yacht Club, built in 1903 at the same location that was
consumed by the 1915 fire that destroyed much of Avalon. The CIYC clubhouse construction
was financed by thirty Avalon boaters who each contributed cash and a promissory note to fully
fund the cost of the design and construction. The designer and architect of the clubhouse was
Harry Vaughn, whose design is instantly recognizable from the harbor entrance because of its
distinctive lighthouse silhouette.

To begin the construction project on the Sophia Yacht Club’s remaining piers, CIYC received a
lease on February 1, 1924, from The Santa Catalina Island Company, as well as permits to build
over the water from the United States Engineers Office of the US War Department March 12,
1924. On February 1, 1943, The Santa Catalina Island Company deeded the property and all of
its improvements back to CIYC and on April 4th, 1946, CIYC entered into its historic first lease
with the City of Avalon. Except for a brief period during the war years of 1942-’45, when it was
occupied by the Merchant Marine and used as a training facility, the Club has operated
continuously ever since its first opening day on August 24, 1924.

Today club membership is limited to 180 members due to capacity limitations but enjoys a
membership considerably more diverse than its early days. Boating enthusiasm and a love for
the Island and the Avalon community are essential membership characteristics.

Background of CIYC’s Stewardship and Occupancy of the Clubhouse

CIYC’s current occupancy is pursuant to a 1995 lease agreement which was amended and
extended in 2017 (referred to as the “2017 Amendment”). The 2017 Amendment has a term
extending through July 2023. The 2017 Amendment includes an option for the CIYC to extend
the lease through September 2033, with notice of such extension being required by September
2022.
 Consistent with prior lease agreements for the Clubhouse, the 1995 lease agreement, as
amended in 2017, is a ‘triple net ease” for the City of Avalon, under which CIYC is obligated to
pay for all taxes, insurance premiums, operating charges, maintenance charges, construction
costs and any other costs related to the use/occupancy of the Clubhouse.

Over its 98-year occupancy, the costs borne by CIYC have grown dramatically and have
generally outpaced inflation. The primary reason for this escalation is the aging of the
Clubhouse. As would be expected, any structure that is nearly 100 years old and which is built
on a piling structure overhanging the water generates a need for substantial ongoing
maintenance to ensure upkeep, stability and safety. These maintenance requirements are, of
course, only exacerbated by the fact that Avalon’s Harbor, and therefore the Clubhouse, is
seasonally subjected to strong “nor’easter” conditions. Such storms generate large surge and
waves into the Clubhouse’s piling, decking and float structures.

Due to this risk, all of the pre-existing timber pilings were strengthen over a 10-year period at a
cost of $1,100,000. The strengthening was completed in 2011 and consisted of carbon fiber
jacketing wrapped around the pilings, then filled with specialized cement fill to create a
composite structure capable of resisting decay and deterioration while furnishing the necessary
bearing support. In more recent years, the piling connection plates and brackets between the
piling and the support timbers are being replaced with corrosion resistant material. The
structure beneath the club will continue to require substantial refurbishment. These costs
include licensing/permitting contractors for diving services to redo piling base and tooting
areas, contractors to refurb/repair the pilings themselves and other requirements such as eel
grass surveys etc. It is envisioned that CIYC will continue to incur costs at a substantial level
moving forward to continue this work. While the costs will vary from year to year, it is expected
that the Clubhouse piling/decking structure will require from $10,000 to over $50,000 each
year for at least the next 6-8 years. It is possible that the costs could dramatically increase from
those levels if a large storm were to cause substantial damage.

In addition to the costs to maintain the piling/decking structure supporting the Clubhouse
above the water, Cl/C also incurs costs for normal periodic maintenance for the Clubhouse and
float structure. Generally speaking, these costs run at least $25,000- $100,000 annually. As an
example, in 2020/2021 over $145,000 was expended to repair dry rot, termite damage and to
paint the exterior of the building. Upgrades to the Clubhouse interior are also frequently
undertaken. In 2019, S60,000 was expended for the remodel of the kitchen, Boatique, and
former apartment.

Insurance costs for the Clubhouse have also increased very dramatically over the past several
years. For 2021 the Cl/C expended over $90,000 in premiums for the necessary insurance
coverage package for the Clubhouse. Included therein was approximately $45,000 for flood
insurance which, alone, has increased from an approximate premium level of S18,000 in 2016.

The heavy rains that impacted Avalon in 2019, caused the hillside above the clubhouse to slide
and block Casino way for a period of time. This blockage seriously impacted access for
 emergency vehicles to the Dive Park, the Casino, Hamilton Cove and Descanso Beach Club. CIYC
has allocated $160,000 to install a retaining wall that would be designed to (I) substantially
mitigate the risk of road closure due to such slides; (ii) protect the clubhouse from slide
damage; and (Hi) expand available club and public parking in the area.
The Role of CIYC in Avalon’s Community and Economy

The Role of CIVC in Avalon’s Community and Economy

The CIYC and its members have, over the entire course if its history, placed a strong emphasis
on being positive contributors to the economy, culture and social fabric of Avalon and Santa
Catalina Island.

While separate from CIYC itself, the CIYC Foundation (“The Foundation”) is a charitable not-for-
profit that derives substantially all its funding from CIYC members. The Foundation and
individuals who are members have, over their collective history, been significant contributors to
charitable organizations serving the needs of Avalon and its residents. In 2020 alone, the
Foundation contributed over $33,000 to the Avalon Food Bank and an additional $42,000 to
supplement other programs the City needed to eliminate from its budget during the pandemic,
Other frequent beneficiaries of the Foundation have included the Avalon Choices, Avalon Little
League, Avalon Rotary Club, Avalon Teen Center, Catalina Island Medical Center Foundation,
Kid’s Ventures and the Museum, among others. At various points, college scholarship funds
were provided by the Foundation and the CIYC membership for graduates of Avalon schools.

CIVC members individually support several of these same causes along with the Chamber of
Commerce and many others. The CIYC, its members and the Foundation are committed to
continuing our 98-year history of supporting philanthropic causes which aid Avalon in providing
opportunities for its residents.

The CIYC also supports allowing the public to experience the historic Clubhouse and its
contents. The Clubhouse houses a comprehensive collection and archive of memorabilia from
the historic yachting history of the Club and its members, including photographs, books,
trophies and artifacts. For many years, CIYC has hosted tours, luncheons and dinners for guests.

The CIYC and the Foundation are also significant contributors to Avalon’s economy via a
plethora of avenues. Annually, CIYC hosts between 18 to 24 large banquets, which provide
$35,000 to $50,000 of event catering revenues to local Avalon restaurants and caterers. The
Clubhouse is utilized weekly by members and their families during the entire year and, of
course, these groups provide substantial guest traffic for Avalon bars and restaurants; the
Avalon Golf Course; Taxi services; tourism activities such as inland tours, mooring rentals, golf
cart rentals and Catalina Express boat tickets.

CIYC members also contribute to the Avalon community through the traditional tax base as
owners of over 71 moorings and several local Avalon properties that pay property taxes.
Additionally, we believe that the existence of the club and its activities in Avalon drive the
 values of mooring in the harbor to further build that significant tax base for services in the
community.

Additionally, the ongoing maintenance of the Clubhouse and its float structure utilize the
services of many local Avalon vendors including the Catalina Boatyard, Chet’s Hardware Store,
Pebbly Beach Building Supply, Island Janitorial, Avalon Fire Extinguishers, Catalina Plumbing,
local painters, and laborers etc. And, of course, CIYC members utilize services for boat repairs,
the fuel dock and the like.

The CIYC, its Board of Directors and its members view our history and our future as intertwined
with that of Avalon and Catalina Island. CIYC is simply not the same institution without its close
association with Avalon. The members of CIYC remain deeply committed to playing a positive
contributing role to the economy, culture and tourism prospects of Avalon.

The CIYC’s Goal for Long-Term Partnership with the City of Avalon

As discussed above, CIYC views its future with Avalon with a long-term perspective.
Furthermore, CIYC is committed to continuing the substantial annual financial expenditures
necessary to maintain the long-term stability and safety of the Clubhouse. However, as we
approach the end of our lease commitment with the City of Avalon, it will grow increasingly
challenging to justify making these sizable investments in the Clubhouse’s long-term future.

Hence, CIYC wishes to commit to a new long-term lease for the Clubhouse with a 20-year term,
plus two 10-year extension periods. We believe that this would be highly beneficial for the City
of Avalon as well. The CIYC Board of Directors are ready to engage with the Cfty Council and City
Manager whenever permitted to do so.

Thank you for your attention and we look forward to speaking with you soon. Roland Rapp is
the Chairman of our Board of Directors and will serve as the point person for The CIYC on this
process.

multimodal transportation strategy to reduce reliance on personal motor vehicles, enhance the

businesses.

engineering group and regularly perform transportation studies for the City. W-Trans submitted
a proposal for $149,975. Staff is requesting a not to exceed authorization of $160,000 to allow
for any contingencies. The grant was awarded for $173,519 with a S23.641 matching
requirement for a total project budget of $197,000.

SUBJECT:  Fiscal Year 2022-2023 Miscellaneous Fee Schedule Workshop

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): 1. Open the Public Hearing to hear public comments. 2. Close
the Public Hearing. 3. Discuss and determine an appropriate fee increase. 4.
If consensus, adopt the fee schedule.

REPORT SUMMARY: The City charges fees for miscellaneous public services, facility
use/rental and activities. User fees are assessed and collected for City services and programs
provided by various departments including:

  •  Recreation programs and facilities
  •  Planning & building (reviews, inspections, variances, etc.)
  •  Fire, Law Enforcement, Code Enforcement
  •  Harbor operations and activities
  •  Cemetery
  •  Finance/Administrative Services
  •  Public Works

These are services that convey a benefit, grant a privilege, provide for review and enforcement
of regulatory activities, enforce laws or are a condition of development. Under
State law, cities may charge fees to recoup the direct and indirect costs related to the provision
of user services.

Ideally, each year, cities should review their fees to establish new fees, modify existing fees! and
eliminate fees that are no longer required to ensure that City fees are in line with the costs
incurred to provide them. In Fiscal Year 2021-22, City Council approved a 2.48% increase for
the majority of fees, with the exception transit fees and certain recreation fees. The percentage
increase was based on the consumer price index (CR) information provided by the Bureau of
Labor Statistics for Los Angeles County based on the latest available fiscal year information.
Using the CPI as an average cost increase annually ensures the city does not unnecessarily
burden the citizens with unusually large spikes in fees while also ensuring that the City continues
to recoup costs associated with the increased costs to provide these services.

Staff recommends increasing the majority of fees based on the latest available calendar year
CPI information provided by the Bureau of Labor Statistics for Los Angeles County which shows
 an increase of 5.07% based on the second half of 2021! with the fees rounded to the nearest
dollar.

The following fees are new to the fee schedule or increased by an amount other than CPI:

  •  Ambulance service fees set based on Los Angeles County Emergency Medical Services
  Agency Rate Schedule
  •  No proposed increase to fixed route and dial-a-ride transit fees
  •  Day Camp daily and weekly fee increase does not go into effect until Summer 2023 to
  avoid rate increases mid-program.

Based on Council’s prior direction! Staff plans to reassess the vehicle permit fees, currently
increased by CPI, to ensure the fees are sufficient to cover the costs associated with vehicle
permitting and enforcement during the upcoming fiscal year prior to the start of vehicle
registration in 2023. In addition! Staff is reassessing the transient rental licensing fee, which
replaced the Conditional Use Permit process for transient rentals and will present the updated
fee and its annual renewal for Council consideration and adOption during the upcoming fiscal
year.

Notice of the public hearing was published in accordance with the applicable law.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: City costs will be offset by annual revenues.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Staff estimates that should general City fees be increased by the
recommended amounts, annual revenue of approximately $50,000 in the General Fund and
$100,000 in Harbor Fund revenues would be generated! offset by cost increases to City
operations.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The costs of special
services will not be fully funded by fees paid by the users of those services. The unfunded
portion of user services will be subsidized by General City tax revenues and/or available fund
balances.

FOLLOW UP ACTION:  Adopt the attached resolution establishing city rates and fees for
services.

Section 15301 of the State CEQA Guidelines— Existing Facilities.

The April 20, 2022 meeting was the fourth time the Planning Commission heard an issue
regarding the 261 E. Whittley Property:
  -  July 17, 2019 A Public Hearing was conducted for Site Plan review to renovate an
  —

  existing duplex with four bedrooms into a four bedroom single family dwelling. The project
  included the addition of 974 square feet.
  -  November 20, 2019 Application for a Site Plan, Height Variance (for a chimney) and
  —

  —

  via PC Resolution No. 22-08, which approved the Variance and Site Plan while finding
  the project exempt from environmental review.

Commission on November 20, 2019 included the remodel of an existing nonconforming structure
encroaching up to three (3) feet of the rear property line and directly adjacent to the western
property line, where the standard setback requirement for this zone is ten (10) feet. The
subsequent new construction maintains a three (3) foot setback. The original construction plan
included remodeling the rear property with the intent of maintaining its nonconforming status.
However, after issued a building permit on September 14, 2021, it was determined that the
 necessary improvements to retain the second building were infeasible, and the entire structure
was demolished. The owner’s intent was to move forward with the construction as previously
reviewed and approved.

AMC 9-8.703 (a) establishes: “A nonconforming building or structure may be continuously
maintained provided there is no alteration, addition or enlargement of any area, space or volume
of the structure  As the approved, necessary improvements were considered infeasible
without demolition of the structure, Staff recommendation to the Planning Commission during
the March 16, 2022 and April 20,2022 meetings maintained that the renovated building complies
with AMC 9-8.703 (a). The Planning Commission accepted Staff’s recommendation, approved
the Site Plan and Setback Variance by Resolution 22-08.

On May 3, 2022 Charles Canby, and other surrounding property owners, filed a timely appeal of
the Planning Commission’s decision, requesting that the City Council hear the Project de novo
at a public hearing.

Article 8.6 of the Planning and Zoning Code (“Appeals”) states:

  a) Within 15 days after the receipt by the applicant for a variance or conditional use permit,
  or receipt by the owner or operator of a use which was the subject of a public hearing for
  revocation or modification, or notice of the action of the Commission, any person
  dissatisfied with the action of the Commission may file with the City Clerk an appeal from

  1. Affirm the action of the Commission; or
  2. Require a transcript or recording of the testimony, and all other evidence upon
  which the Commission made its decision, and after receiving such evidence take
  such action as, in its opinion, is indicated by such evidence alone; or
  3. Refer the matter back to the Commission, with or without instructions for further
  proceedings; or
  4. Set the matter for hearing before itself. At such hearing, it shall hear and decide
  the case de novo.

April 14, 2022

To: City of Avalon Planning Commission Members and Staff

From: Charles Canby, 242 Whittley Aye, Avalon, CA

Subject: 261 East Whittley, granting of variance for setback.

I am against the Planning Commission granting a set back variance for the noted property.

  1.  I feel that we, residents of our neighborhood, have an expectation that planning and zoning
  rules will be followed and variances should not be granted to accommodate another person’s
  personal gains, desires and whims when they are unwarranted and to the detriment of others.

  2.  The proposed variance will shade the adjoining neighbors’ yards and homes and, will put a
  twenty-foot-high structure within three feet of their yards and view, and go against their
  expectation that when purchasing their property, buildings behind them would have a ten-foot
  set-back.

  3.  I have reviewed the plans for this project and looked over the property to gain an understanding
  of the project.

  4.  The area/yard where the Vaneverys want to build is a huge area with plenty of square footage.
  It is easily large enough to build a very large structure of equal square footage that they desire
  and still have open space for a yard without encroaching into the required ten-foot set back.

  5.  The Vaneverys want to encroach into the required setback. I speculate that they want to do so
  for a couple of reasons: First, to have a clear view of the ocean down the back lots of homes on
  East Whittley. Second, to not have to excavate or notch into the sloping hill side of their
  downhill sloping back yard.

  6.  All of the existing homes on East Whittley have maintained the required ten-foot set back.
  Granting this variance could start a precedence.

  7.  The Staff report said “c) The Granting of this Variance will not be detrimental to the public
  welfare or neighborhood property because: The structural footprint will remain almost exactly
  as it has existed since original construction.” The short comings of this statement are: First,
  there are no original drawing or documentation showing the original construction. Second, the
  original structure was said to be much smaller and lower in elevation, and was not twenty feet
  high and three feet from the neighbors back yards. The old structure could not be seen from
  the back yards of the Warrens and Franks.

  8.  The set-back of the old demolished building was “non-conforming”. Now is an opportunity to
  build a conforming building without variances.
